extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, taxonomists, museum curators, medical researchers, and public-health/medical administrators (readers of Nature)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for doing and organising scientific research, taxonomy, physiological experimentation, and public-health administration — including what to report, how to interpret experiments, and how governments/collections should support science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Linnean system to express systematic opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantage of using the Linnean system ... is that it enables the naturalist who has made a special study of a genus to express his opinion, by the arrangement of the specimens into specific groups, of the relations he believes they bear to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematics should allow the worker to arrange specimens into specific groups to express hypotheses about relationships; the stimulus to careful and accurate observation provided by such arrangement is 'the very soul' of systematic zoology. Anti-pattern: presenting only bare facts without arrangement and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogues should include author's thoughts and systematic plans
rubrics_metrics.description: In Mr. Bernard's catalogues we find simply a bald statement of facts ... there is not one word concerning the thoughts or opinions of the man who has devoted so considerable a part of a lifetime to the collection of these facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A catalogue or monograph should not be a mere list of descriptions, figures, tables and lists; it should communicate the author's interpretative judgements and systematic arrangements (an 'architect's plan' rather than a 'quantity surveyor's estimate'). Anti-pattern: discouraging to future workers by offering only unorganized facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active curation: arrange collections into systematic groups
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be a serious mistake if those in charge of collections of corals were contented to adopt the non possumus attitude of Mr. Bernard and make no serious attempt to arrange their specimens in systematic groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curators and collection managers should proactively organize and arrange specimens into systematic groups to make collections useful for systematics; passivity in curation (doing nothing) undermines future systematic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic research must include extensive anatomical study (soft parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic study of the soft parts of a large number of specimens of some one genus ... and a comparison made of the relation of the anatomy of the zoœids to the different forms of skeletal growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should sample many specimens and study soft-part anatomy alongside skeletal characters to distinguish intrinsic/heritable characters from environmentally induced ones and thereby identify characters of true taxonomic value. Some of existing tables may be useful but much original rework will be required for systematic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate geographic variation and correlate characters
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems to be a fairly constant difference between the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific specimens of Porites ... the trabecular, horizontal and synapticular elements ... are thicker and coarser in the Atlantic and West Indian forms than they are in those of the Indo-Pacific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When geographic differences are observed in skeletal characters, researchers should investigate whether anatomical (soft-part) characters coincide with skeletal differences before rearranging species. Exceptions require special investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State assumptions and consider alternatives in quantitative calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be assumed that the whole of the kinetic energy of the α particles ... appears as heat energy, the value for m is found to be ... I have thought it best to give the maximum estimate of that quantity which can be attained by this method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deriving physical quantities from indirect measures, explicitly state assumptions (e.g., all kinetic energy becomes heat), perform calculations accordingly, and provide alternative estimates under different assumptions; discuss how results support or refute competing hypotheses (e.g., helium atom vs hydrogen molecule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret experimental results in the context of whether conditions are normal or abnormal
rubrics_metrics.description: These recent experiments have clearly shown that the 'renal-portal' circulation will not yield the slightest secretion in the absence of powerful diuretics; in other words, the result obtained ... is at best an abnormal one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimental manipulations (e.g., elimination of arterial supply, forced injection, use of powerful diuretics) produce effects, assess whether those results reflect normal physiology or artefacts of abnormal conditions. Do not generalize from results obtained only under forced/abnormal setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for artefacts (degeneration, pressure, perfusion) when inferring function
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole objection ... was that ... the tubular epithelium had degenerated, and was therefore not in a condition to secrete ... in experiments in which at all large secretions were obtained the pressure was artificially raised by forced injection or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tissue degeneration from lack of oxygen, artificially elevated pressures, and other procedural artefacts that can produce false positives/negatives; explain how these factors could produce observed effects without reflecting normal function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer function from mere structural continuity without histological evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It has always surprised me ... that physiologists have so readily assumed that they possess ... so many convenient anatomical contrivances in which the glomeruli and the renal tubules are supplied by separate vessels. It is true that the renal cardinal meshwork is continuous with the blood plexus surrounding the tubules, but surely it is very unsafe to assume from this one fact that the venous blood is used by the tubules for secretory purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural continuity (vessel continuity) alone does not prove functional contact; require histological and physiological evidence that blood from a given vessel actually contacts and supplies the tubule plexus before asserting excretory function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple lines of evidence to support physiological-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: I supported by citing the physiological experiments of Fussbaum and Beddard ... these experiments proved that after the arterial supply of the frog's kidney had been eliminated all secretion immediately stopped ... I find additional physiological evidence ... British Association Report ... it is shown to be exceedingly probable, by the relative amounts of oxygen used up ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine developmental, structural, histological, physiological experiment, perfusion/oxygen-consumption data and corroborating studies to build robust functional claims; reconcile apparently contradictory results by examining experimental contexts and methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish whether Mendelian laws apply to individuals or to mass statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mendel's laws ... are really mass-laws and not laws of the individual ... Mendel's laws are based on definite conceptions as to the germ-cells of the individual — and that is the important point — and are true of the individual to a degree of approximation which is the higher the greater the number of offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about genetic laws, be explicit whether claims concern the behaviour of individual germ-cells/organisms or statistical regularities in large ensembles; theoretical assertions should be linked to what is empirically testable at the individual vs population level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically test whether a Mendelian unit shows heritable individual variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The question ... whether a unit Mendelian character exhibits heritable individual variations or no seems to be one that urgently calls for experimental investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and carry out targeted experiments to determine whether supposed Mendelian units are themselves subject to heritable continuous variation; avoid assuming either side without empirical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific administration requires exact knowledge and efficient organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Such concerted action is likely to be successful only when it is based on sufficient knowledge; and a scientific administration differs from an unscientific one just in this particular, that it seeks the necessary knowledge, while the other acts blindly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health or governmental departments must (1) obtain exact knowledge of disease causation and control, and (2) have efficient organisational structures to act on that knowledge; both elements are indispensable for effective public welfare action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should fund and carry out organised research into prevalent diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: Why did not Government carry on much more extensive researches? The time-worn answer always was, because they could not afford it. But, surely, if they could afford such a large and expensive medical establishment, they should also be able to afford those researches which were essential to making that establishment effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deferring research for alleged lack of funds when medical establishments exist; prioritise and allocate government funds to systematic, official investigations (permanent laboratories, commissions) into major diseases rather than relying solely on individual initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make effective use of available medical staff for research and provide incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: The authorities could have had almost for nothing scores of enthusiastic and, I will expressly add, capable workers ... A microscope, a few test-tubes, a word from the chief, a little approbation, some evidence that scientific work leads, if successful, to preferment, and the authorities could have had ... workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilise underemployed junior medical officers for research by providing minimal equipment, encouragement, time/leave, and clear career incentives (preferment tied to scientific achievement) instead of discouraging voluntary investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide access to recent scientific literature and necessary laboratory equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: That first essential, recent scientific literature, was most difficult of access, and the authorities still seem to have made no adequate attempt to improve matters. Microscopes and bacteriological apparatus were generally wanting, although they are absolutely necessary in tropical clinical practice ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative bodies must ensure staff have access to up-to-date scientific literature and essential instruments (microscopes, bacteriological apparatus) required for modern clinical diagnosis and research, especially in regions with specific endemic diseases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base appointments and promotion on scientific and professional ability, not favour
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual 'Records of Service' ... was a hopelessly stupid form which made no attempt to distinguish their real scientific and professional ability— so that ... appointments ... went by favour!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement fair, merit-based promotion systems including examinations, documented scientific contributions, and objective assessment of research/clinical competence to encourage and reward genuine scientific work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorities must promptly investigate and implement important scientific discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Koch discovered the cause of cholera ... Hankin carried out his admirable researches ... This again should have received close official scrutiny with a view to its general adoption or rejection ... Typhoid ... has never received adequate official inquiry ... Manson's discovery ... has never ... been followed by sufficient practical action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When credible discoveries about disease causation or prevention are made (cholera, malaria, mosquito vectors, well treatment), governments should immediately commission official scrutiny, field trials, and, where appropriate, adopt preventive measures rather than neglect or fail to acknowledge contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish permanent laboratories and follow-up official inquiries for major public-health problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary inquiries had been made ... but these were obviously insufficient to enlighten us on the multitude of strange and mysterious diseases we were called upon to deal with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term, ad-hoc inquiries are inadequate; governments should establish ongoing, well-resourced laboratories and official inquiry mechanisms to continually investigate endemic and epidemic diseases and to translate research into policy and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wasteful allocation; reallocate resources to essential research
rubrics_metrics.description: Huge sums, which would pay for such research for years, were being spent on engineering works of only local value. Even within the medical budget, money was being wasted on certain sinecures and useless administrative posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct budgetary review and prioritize funding for research and scientific infrastructure over low-priority projects and sinecures; an inefficient administrative machine is ultimately more expensive and less protective of public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that lack of organised research undermines epidemic control
rubrics_metrics.description: An inefficient machine is the most expensive of all ... Without such information the work of the department was largely useless ... The time-worn answer ... 'no funds' was palpably untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health responses to epidemics must be grounded in organised research; failing to invest in research and implement findings will impair prevention and control efforts and cost lives.
